title: Ancient Trees in Estonia: Cities to Explore
meta_description: Estonia printed its thickest tree on a banknote: the Tamme-Lauri oak, 8.31 metres round. {cities} cities mapped, {trees} trees.
intro: Estonia put a tree on its money. The Tamme-Lauri Oak in Urvaste, 8.31 metres round at chest height and dated by a 1998 ring study to 1326, was printed on the back of the old 10 kroon note, and it is the country's thickest tree. The largest by volume is not an oak at all: the King's Pine in Järvselja, over 33 metres tall. Most of what you can walk to is in Tallinn, where the stories are small ones: a ginkgo that stopped a Soviet grandstand, an oak that moved a coastal road, and lindens planted in 1883 to mark two centuries of one family at one address. Tallinn's thickest, the Tammesalu Oak, was already sizeable when Peter the Great bought its land in 1714. Four places mapped so far, twelve trees, from a banknote oak in the south to a ginkgo on a city corner.
